Linux OPPE Question - Question 1

Problem Statement

Given a list of filenames (with extensions), one per line, write a script that counts the number of files for each file extension and outputs the results in the format given below. The output should be sorted by descending count of files, and then by descending order of the file extension.

Instructions

  • Write your script in script.sh file, it should be executable by your user.
  • It should read input from standard input and write output to standard output.
  • No actual files will be created or accessed; the script should only process the provided input.

Sample Input

hello.txt
bye.pdf
cats.txt
video.mp4
music.mp3
document.docx
list.txt
song.mp3
movie.MP4

Sample Output

      3 .txt
      2 .mp4
      2 .mp3
      1 .pdf
      1 .docx

Constraints

  • The filenames will always contain an extension (i.e., there will be at least one dot in the filename).
  • The extensions may be in either case (e.g., .TXT and .txt should be considered the same extension).
  • The output must be in lowercase.

Hints

  • Simply sorting the entire output line in descending order will work, given it handles numbers correctly.

Linux OPPE Question - Question 2

Motivation

Two numbers are called twin-prime if both are prime, and they differ by 2. For example, (3, 5) and (11, 13) are twin-prime pairs.

Problem Statement

Given a number n, find all twin-prime pairs whose sum is less than or equal to n.

Instructions

  • Write your script in script.sh.
  • The script should be executable by your user.
  • Read n from standard input.
  • Print each twin-prime pair on a new line in the format (p1, p2) where p1 and p2 are the twin primes on separate lines.

Sample Input

24

Sample Output

(3, 5)
(5, 7)
(11, 13)

Constraints

  • n will be a positive integer less than or equal to 10000.
  • Each pair should be ordered such that the smaller prime comes first (i.e., (3, 5) and not (5, 3)).
  • The output should be sorted in ascending order based on the first prime in the pair.

Hints

  • It is mathematically guaranteed that twin prime numbers are odd. (Think why?)

Linux OPPE Question - Question 3

Motivation

sha1sum is a common utility used to compute and verify SHA-1 hashes. It is often used to ensure the integrity of files by comparing the computed hash with a known hash value.

A hash function takes an input (or ‘message’) and returns a fixed-size string of bytes. The output is typically a ‘digest’ that is unique to each unique input. Even a small change in the input will produce a significantly different hash. Of course, by pigeon-hole principle, there are many different inputs that can produce the same hash (called a ‘collision’), but it is computationally infeasible to find two different inputs that produce the same hash. For bigger hashes (like SHA-256), the probability of collisions is even lower.

> sha1sum <<< "hello world"
22596363b3de40b06f981fb85d82312e8c0ed511  -

> sha1sum <<< "hello universe" | cut -d' ' -f1
f6b4cf7824a46af518b7f06b53d660a0a39e7634

Problem Statement

You want to play a game – given a string, you want to find whether the SHA-1 hash of the string contains the string in it or not. Further, if it does not contain the string, you then take the SHA-1 hash of the hash, and continue the process until you find a hash that contains the original string or you have done it 10 times. In each iteration, print the iteration number and the hash. If you find a hash that contains the original string, stop iterating. If after 10 iterations you do not find a hash that contains the original string, print “Not Found”.

It is trivial to note that if the input contains non-hexadecimal characters, it cannot be found in the hash ever (since SHA-1 hashes comprise of only hexadecimal characters), so you should immediately print “Not Found” in that case and not perform any iteration.

Instructions

  • Write your script in script.sh.
  • The script should read a single line of input from standard input, which will be the string to be checked.
  • The script should output the iteration number and the corresponding hash for each iteration, and if a hash containing the original string is found, it should stop iterating. If after 10 iterations no such hash is found, it should print “Not Found”.
  • The script should handle the case where the input string contains non-hexadecimal characters by immediately printing “Not Found” and exiting.
  • The script should be executable by your user.

Sample Input 1

12

Sample Output 1

2: ab16bf05b01c833603826780711e0012597f02d7

2: 8e1aff27c58e3d48447d7d7b681594ec9f15758c
3: 5543dd199a878b122a6ba06c812c823e2dad9f47

9: 1142b780c81092b3051f5c08d27001b1274ab4e8
10: 77bae33f58a2ef97eb1d356238a679e2e0bc4b05
Not Found

Sample Input 3

Sample Output 3

Constraints

  • The input string can be of any length, but it will only contain printable alphanumeric characters.
  • The check should be case-insensitive.

Linux OPPE Question - Question 4

Problem Statement

You are given a log file containing multiple lines of logs. Each line contains a single log entry from your system in the following format:

YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS [LOG_LEVEL] Message

Where:

  • YYYY-MM-DD is the date of the log entry.
  • HH:MM:SS is the time of the log entry.
  • LOG_LEVEL is the severity level of the log (e.g., INFO, WARNING, ERROR).
  • Message is the actual log message.

Write a sed script to print out only the ERROR messages from the log files. Remove the log level from the messages since they are all ERROR messages. The output should only contain the date, time, and the message.

Instructions

  • Write your script in script.sed file.
  • It should be a sed script, not a bash script.
  • The script will be executed against the input as follows:
sed -Ef script.sed < input.log

Linux OPPE Question - Question 5

Motivation

CSV Handling

In awk, we can set the field separator and output field separator to any character by overriding the built-in variables FS and OFS.

BEGIN {
  FS=":"
  OFS="-"
}

Associative Arrays

Awk supports associative arrays, which allow us to use strings as keys. This is particularly useful for counting occurrences or mapping values.

{
  count[$1]++
  map[$1] = $2
}
END {
  for (key in count) {
    print key, map[key], count[key]
  }
}

Problem Statement

You are given a CSV input where each line contains details of an employee in the following format:

id,name,manager_id

Where:

  • id is a unique identifier for the employee.
  • name is the name of the employee.
  • manager_id is the unique identifier of the employee’s manager. If the employee has no manager, this field will be 0.

Output a different CSV which contains each employee’s details along with how many direct reports they have. The output format should be:

id,name,direct_subordinates

Where direct_subordinates is the count of employees that report directly to the manager.

Instructions

  • Write your solution in a file named script.awk.
  • The solution should be an awk script, not a shell script.
  • It will be run as follows:
gawk -f script.awk < input.csv

Sample Input

1,Alice,0
2,Bob,3
3,Charlie,1
4,Don,1

Sample Output

1,Alice,2
2,Bob,0
3,Charlie,1
4,Don,0

Constraints

  • The input CSV will NOT have a header line.
  • The output CSV should NOT have a header line.
  • The id and manager_id fields will always be integers.
  • The name field will always be a string without commas.
  • The manager_id values are guaranteed to be valid id values or 0.
  • There will be no duplicates in the id field.

accepted_answer.excerpt:
I can understand all of your sentiments, and it is not disregarded. However we are familiar with this sentiment each term: “OPPE was harder than last term”, which obviously cannot (and is not) true. The phenomenon that happens is that:

  • You are practising NPPE in a relaxed manner without time limits and can refer other resources; where-as OPPE is a high stress environment without any external reference, ChatGPT to help you understand how a syntax works, etc.
  • In this case your ability to debug logical and syntax issues natively comes into play, which can only work if you use these tools regularly and inculcate your debugging skills. You also need to be familiar with how the evaluation works in general (synchro eval, how diff works, etc).
  • Some of you are not used to the linux mindset yet, and try to translate your imperative thinking into shell scripts instead of doing this the simple way, this is not python or C, this is linux where you are expected to use tools that already exist, not re-invent the wheel.

Case in point:

23f3003894:

Q1. Loop - read line - extract extension using - maintain array and count to increase upon next appearance of same extension.

Outside loop another loop to iterate over the array and just print as per the output req.

It was a simple one line solution which we had exactly discussed in our last session:

grep '\..*$' -o | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

However you would not be able to come up with this if you do not move away from the imperative programming mindset like other languages. That comes with practice, lots of practice.

23f3003894:

Q4. Search for a pattern beginning with [ and ending with a space and substitute with nothing.

This terms’ Q4 was one of the easiest Q4 in last few terms ever, if you are familiar with sed and how it works, and are able to read and understand the problem statement clearly, it is very simple two lines solution:

  • delete all lines that dont have ERROR
  • remove the [ERROR] part using s
/\[ERROR\]/!d
s/\[ERROR\] //

Let me go further and explain the other solutions too once we are at it, this will help you understand whether the questions were hard or you had made the logic overly complicated while trying to solve it.

Q5: we had discussed this directly in our last session how to use associative array to store counts and maps, it is as simple as:

  • store the count of manager ids you encounter
  • map the id to name
  • in the end print each id, name, manager count

Awk makes it trivially simple.

There is a reason we ask questions like this for awk, and not for other tools/languages, because this is where awk shines and makes the script pretty simple. But you can only appreciate this if you think in terms of awk and write awk scripts like they are meant to. If you try to simply think of the logic in python and then translate to awk syntax, it will seem complicated. Rather you should think how an awk programmer would think, that is where it becomes easy. This is a skill which takes time to master.

Sol:

BEGIN{
  FS=","
  OFS=","
}

{
  manages[$3]++
  name[$1]=$2
}

END{
  for (i in name) {
    print i, name[i], manages[i]+0
  }
}

Qs2: we had discussed how to find if a number is prime or not in the session, in fact we discussed two ways to do it:

  • one with C style logic (because most of you are more familiar with that, however you should AVOID IT)
  • one with the linux way, using factor $n | wc -w, a simple and unix-like way

once you can write a function to find if a number is prime or not, it becomes trivial to find list of twin primes in a range, simple run a loop and check each pair.

#!/usr/bin/env bash

read -r n

prime(){
  local num=$1
  if ((num <= 1)); then
    return 1
  fi
  for ((i=2; i <= num/2; i++)); do
    if ((num % i == 0)); then
      return 1
    fi
  done
  return 0
}

for ((x=3; x <= n/2 - 1; x+=2)); do
  if prime $x && prime $((x+2)); then
    echo "($x, $((x+2)))"
  fi
done

or, a better solution:

read -r n

prime(){
	if [[ $(factor $1 | wc -w) -eq 2 ]]; then
		return 0
	fi
	return 1
}

for ((x=3; x <= n/2 - 1; x+=2)); do
  if prime $x && prime $((x+2)); then
    echo "($x, $((x+2)))"
  fi
done

I dont think these are hard to write or think, but I can understand why it might feel like that in a timeboxed and high-pressure environment if you have not practiced enough and are not confident.

Explanation:

  • twin primes need to have same parity (x and x+2 will always be both even or both odd), and there are no even primes other than 2, so twin primes are odd only (so you can do x+=2 instead of x++ however x++ will also work here)
  • if sum of twin primes is \leq n, then x + (x+2) \leq n \implies x \leq \frac{n}{2} - 1 , however you can also simply do a while true and if (( x + x + 2 > n )); break if you are not able to do the algebric simplification.

Finally, Q3, yes this one is a bit harder than the other 4, which is expected since you cannot be expected to get all 5 questions to be easy.

Although the logic for this too is pretty straight forward:

  • get the string
  • check if it has non hexadecimal digits (non 0-9a-fA-F)
  • run a loop 10 times
  • calculate its sha1sum (we saw in session how to do this, also motivation was given)
  • repeat

Building the syntax for this without syntax errors is the main task of this question, which can be done if:

  • you are profecient with shell scripting syntax
  • you are able to debug output and understand exactly what mistakes you made and how to fix it

again, these come with practice and you cannot expect to suddenly be an expert in this after practising for one week, some of the posts here sound too short-sighted. Practising 1 week for a 12 week course is not enough, especially for a practical and hands-on course like system commands. You need to build the functional programming thinking, and learn totally new tools and syntaxes, which takes time effort and practice.

Anyway, coming to the solution:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
read -r n

if ! [[ "$n" =~ ^[0-9a-fA-F]+$ ]]; then
  echo "Not Found"
  exit 0
fi

sum=$(sha1sum <<< "$n" | cut -d' ' -f1)
for i in {1..10}; do
  echo "$i: $sum"
  if grep -iq "$n" <<< "$sum" ; then
    exit 0
  fi
  sum=$(sha1sum <<< "$sum" | cut -d' ' -f1)
done

echo "Not Found"

The reason I am sharing these solutions is to:

  • maintain transparency between the students and the team, and you know exactly what we expect you to be able to write in the exam in 2 hours (not some elaborate imperative logic with 2 loops etc)
  • demonstrate how the solution could be simple if thought enough, however this needs some practice and a calm mind
  • help people appearing for re-oppe upsolve.

Someone in this thread compared these questions to leetcode questions, well you have the same concept of upsolving in leetcode or any CP. You are of course not expected to be able to solve all questions in first attempt. That would make this a student-placating course, which we are not. Our goal is to instill proper unix-thinking in students and ability to write scripts the unix way, not translate imperative logic into shell syntax. This comes with practice and hardwork, and we will not compromise the quality of the course to avoid the painful journey. Rather, you are expected to upsolve questions you could’nt solve in the timed exam, and understand the solution and be better in the skill.

Also, yes REOPPE will have one or two easy questions, because, afterall it is a lifeline to save you from wasting another term. But it comes with the promise of practice and upsolve, without which you will still not be able to pass.

However, REOPPE is not a wild-card for any/all, (like some are mentioning of tactics to deliberately fail), so some questions in REOPPE will be harder (as we have clarified multiple times in sessions and discourse). So first slot is the best opportunity to score 100, as re-oppe is less likely to score 100.

I hope this reply answers most of your queries which are genuine. We will not be providing any concessions however for this OPPE, and we hope that after you have had some time to cool down and objectively look at the questions and the sample solutions, you realise it is in-fact not that hard, and was quite simple. In the end, difficulty level is a subjective opinion and we will not argue with you on it if you are of a different opinion. However, the take on maintaining course quality is final and would not be compromised with.

Also, I have personally gone through each question and sample solutions, there are no errors in evaluators for any question, and correct solution passes all test cases (public and private) in all 7 VMs (verified multiple times, by different instructors, in all VMs). If your synchro eval gives output which look the same to you, know that diff prints nothing if the two files are identifcal. So the fact something was printed indicates there is a difference. You need to figure out what exactly was not matching (formatting? ordering? etc)

Also, if public test cases pass but private fail, it indicates your code does not handle all edge cases. This is there in all courses and all leetcode/cp etc. That is why we have private test cases, to see if you are able to generalize your logic and handle edge cases or you simply hardcode for the examples given. No concessions are given for people getting 0 private test cases passed. We do not award any marks for passing public test cases. Hopefully this was clarified before the exam too.

I request the TAs to also engage in healthy discussions with the genuine learners interested to learn the solutions and better themselves by discussing the solutions or other possible solutions, topics, etc.

All the best for people attempting re-oppe, hopefully you prepare better this time.

  • Print each twin-prime pair on a new line in the format (p1, p2) where p1 and p2 are the twin primes on separate lines.

(5, 7)
(11, 13)

  • n will be a positive integer less than or equal to 10000.
  • Each pair should be ordered such that the smaller prime comes first (i.e., (3, 5) and not (5, 3)).

Hints

  • It is mathematically guaranteed that twin prime numbers are odd. (Think why?)

Linux OPPE Question - Question 3

Motivation

sha1sum is a common utility used to compute and verify SHA-1 hashes. It is often used to ensure the integrity of files by comparing the computed hash with a known hash value.

A hash function takes an input (or ‘message’) and returns a fixed-size string of bytes. The output is typically a ‘digest’ that is unique to each unique input. Even a small change in the input will produce a significantly different hash. Of course, by pigeon-hole principle, there are many different inputs that can produce the same hash (called a ‘collision’), but it is computationally infeasible to find two different inputs that produce the same hash. For bigger hashes (like SHA-256), the probability of collisions is even lower.

> sha1sum <<< "hello world"
22596363b3de40b06f981fb85d82312e8c0ed511  -

> sha1sum <<< "hello universe" | cut -d' ' -f1
f6b4cf7824a46af518b7f06b53d660a0a39e7634

Problem Statement

You want to play a game – given a string, you want to find whether the SHA-1 hash of the string contains the string in it or not. Further, if it does not contain the string, you then take the SHA-1 hash of the hash, and continue the process until you find a hash that contains the original string or you have done it 10 times. In each iteration, print the iteration number and the hash. If you find a hash that contains the original string, stop iterating. If after 10 iterations you do not find a hash that contains the original string, print “Not Found”.

It is trivial to note that if the input contains non-hexadecimal characters, it cannot be found in the hash ever (since SHA-1 hashes comprise of only hexadecimal characters), so you should immediately print “Not Found” in that case and not perform any iteration.

Instructions

  • Write your script in script.sh.
  • The script should read a single line of input from standard input, which will be the string to be checked.
  • The script should output the iteration number and the corresponding hash for each iteration, and if a hash containing the original string is found, it should stop iterating. If after 10 iterations no such hash is found, it should print “Not Found”.
  • The script should handle the case where the input string contains non-hexadecimal characters by immediately printing “Not Found” and exiting.
  • The script should be executable by your user.

Problem Statement

You are given a log file containing multiple lines of logs. Each line contains a single log entry from your system in the following format:

YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS [LOG_LEVEL] Message

Where:

  • YYYY-MM-DD is the date of the log entry.
  • HH:MM:SS is the time of the log entry.
  • LOG_LEVEL is the severity level of the log (e.g., INFO, WARNING, ERROR).
  • Message is the actual log message.

Write a sed script to print out only the ERROR messages from the log files. Remove the log level from the messages since they are all ERROR messages. The output should only contain the date, time, and the message.

Instructions

  • Write your script in script.sed file.
  • It should be a sed script, not a bash script.
  • The script will be executed against the input as follows:

Linux OPPE Question - Question 5

Motivation

CSV Handling

In awk, we can set the field separator and output field separator to any character by overriding the built-in variables FS and OFS.

BEGIN {
  FS=":"
  OFS="-"
}

Associative Arrays

Awk supports associative arrays, which allow us to use strings as keys. This is particularly useful for counting occurrences or mapping values.

{
  count[$1]++
  map[$1] = $2
}
END {
  for (key in count) {
    print key, map[key], count[key]
  }
}

Problem Statement

You are given a CSV input where each line contains details of an employee in the following format:

id,name,manager_id

Where:

  • id is a unique identifier for the employee.
  • name is the name of the employee.
  • manager_id is the unique identifier of the employee’s manager. If the employee has no manager, this field will be 0.

Output a different CSV which contains each employee’s details along with how many direct reports they have. The output format should be:

id,name,direct_subordinates

Where direct_subordinates is the count of employees that report directly to the manager.

Instructions

  • Write your solution in a file named script.awk.
  • The solution should be an awk script, not a shell script.
  • It will be run as follows:
gawk -f script.awk < input.csv

2,Bob,3
3,Charlie,1
4,Don,1

2,Bob,0
3,Charlie,1
4,Don,0

Constraints

  • The input CSV will NOT have a header line.
  • The output CSV should NOT have a header line.
  • The id and manager_id fields will always be integers.
  • The name field will always be a string without commas.
  • The manager_id values are guaranteed to be valid id values or 0.
  • There will be no duplicates in the id field.

all_posts.name: Sayan Ghosh
all_posts.cooked:
I can understand all of your sentiments, and it is not disregarded. However we are familiar with this sentiment each term: “OPPE was harder than last term”, which obviously cannot (and is not) true. The phenomenon that happens is that:

  • You are practising NPPE in a relaxed manner without time limits and can refer other resources; where-as OPPE is a high stress environment without any external reference, ChatGPT to help you understand how a syntax works, etc.
  • In this case your ability to debug logical and syntax issues natively comes into play, which can only work if you use these tools regularly and inculcate your debugging skills. You also need to be familiar with how the evaluation works in general (synchro eval, how diff works, etc).
  • Some of you are not used to the linux mindset yet, and try to translate your imperative thinking into shell scripts instead of doing this the simple way, this is not python or C, this is linux where you are expected to use tools that already exist, not re-invent the wheel.

Case in point:

23f3003894:

Q1. Loop - read line - extract extension using - maintain array and count to increase upon next appearance of same extension.

Outside loop another loop to iterate over the array and just print as per the output req.

It was a simple one line solution which we had exactly discussed in our last session:

grep '\..*$' -o | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

However you would not be able to come up with this if you do not move away from the imperative programming mindset like other languages. That comes with practice, lots of practice.

23f3003894:

Q4. Search for a pattern beginning with [ and ending with a space and substitute with nothing.

This terms’ Q4 was one of the easiest Q4 in last few terms ever, if you are familiar with sed and how it works, and are able to read and understand the problem statement clearly, it is very simple two lines solution:

  • delete all lines that dont have ERROR
  • remove the [ERROR] part using s
/\[ERROR\]/!d
s/\[ERROR\] //

Let me go further and explain the other solutions too once we are at it, this will help you understand whether the questions were hard or you had made the logic overly complicated while trying to solve it.

Q5: we had discussed this directly in our last session how to use associative array to store counts and maps, it is as simple as:

  • store the count of manager ids you encounter
  • map the id to name
  • in the end print each id, name, manager count

Awk makes it trivially simple.

There is a reason we ask questions like this for awk, and not for other tools/languages, because this is where awk shines and makes the script pretty simple. But you can only appreciate this if you think in terms of awk and write awk scripts like they are meant to. If you try to simply think of the logic in python and then translate to awk syntax, it will seem complicated. Rather you should think how an awk programmer would think, that is where it becomes easy. This is a skill which takes time to master.

Sol:

BEGIN{
  FS=","
  OFS=","
}

{
  manages[$3]++
  name[$1]=$2
}

END{
  for (i in name) {
    print i, name[i], manages[i]+0
  }
}

Qs2: we had discussed how to find if a number is prime or not in the session, in fact we discussed two ways to do it:

  • one with C style logic (because most of you are more familiar with that, however you should AVOID IT)
  • one with the linux way, using factor $n | wc -w, a simple and unix-like way

once you can write a function to find if a number is prime or not, it becomes trivial to find list of twin primes in a range, simple run a loop and check each pair.

#!/usr/bin/env bash

read -r n

prime(){
  local num=$1
  if ((num <= 1)); then
    return 1
  fi
  for ((i=2; i <= num/2; i++)); do
    if ((num % i == 0)); then
      return 1
    fi
  done
  return 0
}

for ((x=3; x <= n/2 - 1; x+=2)); do
  if prime $x && prime $((x+2)); then
    echo "($x, $((x+2)))"
  fi
done

or, a better solution:

read -r n

prime(){
	if [[ $(factor $1 | wc -w) -eq 2 ]]; then
		return 0
	fi
	return 1
}

for ((x=3; x <= n/2 - 1; x+=2)); do
  if prime $x && prime $((x+2)); then
    echo "($x, $((x+2)))"
  fi
done

I dont think these are hard to write or think, but I can understand why it might feel like that in a timeboxed and high-pressure environment if you have not practiced enough and are not confident.

Explanation:

  • twin primes need to have same parity (x and x+2 will always be both even or both odd), and there are no even primes other than 2, so twin primes are odd only (so you can do x+=2 instead of x++ however x++ will also work here)
  • if sum of twin primes is \leq n, then x + (x+2) \leq n \implies x \leq \frac{n}{2} - 1 , however you can also simply do a while true and if (( x + x + 2 > n )); break if you are not able to do the algebric simplification.

Finally, Q3, yes this one is a bit harder than the other 4, which is expected since you cannot be expected to get all 5 questions to be easy.

Although the logic for this too is pretty straight forward:

  • get the string
  • check if it has non hexadecimal digits (non 0-9a-fA-F)
  • run a loop 10 times
  • calculate its sha1sum (we saw in session how to do this, also motivation was given)
  • repeat

Building the syntax for this without syntax errors is the main task of this question, which can be done if:

  • you are profecient with shell scripting syntax
  • you are able to debug output and understand exactly what mistakes you made and how to fix it

again, these come with practice and you cannot expect to suddenly be an expert in this after practising for one week, some of the posts here sound too short-sighted. Practising 1 week for a 12 week course is not enough, especially for a practical and hands-on course like system commands. You need to build the functional programming thinking, and learn totally new tools and syntaxes, which takes time effort and practice.

Anyway, coming to the solution:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
read -r n

if ! [[ "$n" =~ ^[0-9a-fA-F]+$ ]]; then
  echo "Not Found"
  exit 0
fi

sum=$(sha1sum <<< "$n" | cut -d' ' -f1)
for i in {1..10}; do
  echo "$i: $sum"
  if grep -iq "$n" <<< "$sum" ; then
    exit 0
  fi
  sum=$(sha1sum <<< "$sum" | cut -d' ' -f1)
done

echo "Not Found"

The reason I am sharing these solutions is to:

  • maintain transparency between the students and the team, and you know exactly what we expect you to be able to write in the exam in 2 hours (not some elaborate imperative logic with 2 loops etc)
  • demonstrate how the solution could be simple if thought enough, however this needs some practice and a calm mind
  • help people appearing for re-oppe upsolve.

Someone in this thread compared these questions to leetcode questions, well you have the same concept of upsolving in leetcode or any CP. You are of course not expected to be able to solve all questions in first attempt. That would make this a student-placating course, which we are not. Our goal is to instill proper unix-thinking in students and ability to write scripts the unix way, not translate imperative logic into shell syntax. This comes with practice and hardwork, and we will not compromise the quality of the course to avoid the painful journey. Rather, you are expected to upsolve questions you could’nt solve in the timed exam, and understand the solution and be better in the skill.

Also, yes REOPPE will have one or two easy questions, because, afterall it is a lifeline to save you from wasting another term. But it comes with the promise of practice and upsolve, without which you will still not be able to pass.

However, REOPPE is not a wild-card for any/all, (like some are mentioning of tactics to deliberately fail), so some questions in REOPPE will be harder (as we have clarified multiple times in sessions and discourse). So first slot is the best opportunity to score 100, as re-oppe is less likely to score 100.

I hope this reply answers most of your queries which are genuine. We will not be providing any concessions however for this OPPE, and we hope that after you have had some time to cool down and objectively look at the questions and the sample solutions, you realise it is in-fact not that hard, and was quite simple. In the end, difficulty level is a subjective opinion and we will not argue with you on it if you are of a different opinion. However, the take on maintaining course quality is final and would not be compromised with.

Also, I have personally gone through each question and sample solutions, there are no errors in evaluators for any question, and correct solution passes all test cases (public and private) in all 7 VMs (verified multiple times, by different instructors, in all VMs). If your synchro eval gives output which look the same to you, know that diff prints nothing if the two files are identifcal. So the fact something was printed indicates there is a difference. You need to figure out what exactly was not matching (formatting? ordering? etc)

Also, if public test cases pass but private fail, it indicates your code does not handle all edge cases. This is there in all courses and all leetcode/cp etc. That is why we have private test cases, to see if you are able to generalize your logic and handle edge cases or you simply hardcode for the examples given. No concessions are given for people getting 0 private test cases passed. We do not award any marks for passing public test cases. Hopefully this was clarified before the exam too.

I request the TAs to also engage in healthy discussions with the genuine learners interested to learn the solutions and better themselves by discussing the solutions or other possible solutions, topics, etc.

All the best for people attempting re-oppe, hopefully you prepare better this time.

all_posts.name: Seema Malik
all_posts.cooked:
I understand the emphasis on developing a “Unix mindset” and using existing tools effectively instead of writing imperative-style solutions. That is a valuable takeaway from the course, and I agree with that objective.

However, I feel there is a mismatch between what is taught and what is being implicitly expected during evaluation.

This course is, for many of us, our first exposure to Linux and a command-line environment. Along with learning problem-solving using tools like grep, sed, and awk, we are simultaneously dealing with several foundational challenges:

  • Adapting to a completely text-based interface

  • Learning shell navigation and command usage

  • Getting comfortable with editors like Vim

  • Understanding permissions, execution, and file systems

  • Learning regular expressions from scratch

  • Using tools like tmux within the VM environment

All of this is already a steep learning curve within a short duration.

In this context, expecting students to also handle evaluation-specific nuances—such as debugging invisible formatting differences using diff, identifying tab vs space mismatches, or accounting for trailing whitespace—feels beyond the scope of what a beginner course should assume.

Additionally, I would like to highlight the difficulty arising from learning Bash scripting itself, which is very different from most programming languages we are familiar with.

Many of us are simultaneously trying to adapt to:

- Bash syntax rules (e.g., no spaces in assignments like “a=5”)

- Different forms of expansion (“var", "(command)”, “$((expression))”)

- Loop and conditional syntax that differs significantly from languages like Python

- Handling strings, slicing, and quoting correctly

- Subtle syntax errors that are hard to debug

These are not just minor differences—they are fundamental shifts in how we write and think about code, and they take time to internalize. It is very easy to make small syntax mistakes that break the entire script, especially under time pressure.

On top of this, there is also a gap between practice difficulty and exam expectations.

While we do practice problems (NPPE), the actual OPPE seems to:

- require higher precision

- include edge cases not emphasized in practice

- expect familiarity with patterns or techniques that were not clearly highlighted as essential

This creates uncertainty about preparation:

- What level of difficulty should we expect?

- Which concepts are core vs optional?

- What degree of formatting precision is required?

Without a clear benchmark or representative examples of exam-level questions, it becomes difficult to prepare effectively.

Finally, I want to emphasize that this is not just about learning for interest. The OPPE carries significant weight in grading, and performance directly impacts CGPA, which in turn affects placements and academic opportunities.

Given this, it would be helpful if:

- Expectations for the exam are made more explicit

- Practice problems better reflect exam difficulty and constraints

- Critical patterns and edge cases are clearly taught rather than implicitly expected

This would allow students to focus their efforts in the right direction and be evaluated more fairly on what has been taught.

all_posts.name: Seema Malik
all_posts.cooked:
I would also like to highlight a well-known cognitive bias called the “curse of knowledge”, which may be contributing to the difference in perception of difficulty.

The curse of knowledge refers to the tendency for individuals who are experienced in a subject to find it difficult to recall what it was like to learn it for the first time. As a result, concepts that now feel intuitive—such as debugging with “diff”, understanding subtle formatting issues, or reasoning about default behaviors in tools like “sed”—may appear “basic” from an experienced perspective.

However, for beginners, these are not yet internalized skills. They require deliberate effort, repeated exposure, and time to develop. At this stage, students are still simultaneously learning multiple foundational aspects of Linux, Bash, and related tools.

This creates a natural gap between:

- what feels straightforward to someone experienced

- and what is realistically manageable for someone still building foundational understanding

Recognizing this gap can help ensure that evaluation expectations are aligned with the learning stage of students, especially in an introductory course.

all_posts.name: Seema Malik
all_posts.cooked:
We can maintain academic rigor and course quality while making evaluation more aligned with learning by adjusting the structure.

For example, having two OPPEs instead of one, as done in other courses, would distribute evaluation more effectively and reduce the pressure of a single high-stakes exam.

Additionally, introducing low-stakes, timed assessments (similar to OPPE format—such as ROE-style tasks) with clear expectations could help simulate the actual exam environment. This would allow students to get familiar with constraints like time pressure, formatting precision, and tool usage without heavy grade penalties.

As mentioned, students often rely on external help like ChatGPT during regular assignments such as GrPA and BPTs. While these are useful for learning, they do not encourage developing the ability to independently debug using tools like “man”, built-in help, and other resources available in the VM.

Having time-bound assessments that require working within the VM using these tools would help build that skill gradually, instead of expecting it only during a high-stakes exam.

Overall, this approach would better prepare students for OPPE while still maintaining the rigor and quality of the course.
